title: Capital Allocation
text:
Allocating capital between risky assets and risk free assets
Possible to split investment funds between safe and risky assets
Risk free asset: proxy; T-bills
Perfectly price-indexed bond – the only risk free asset in real terms;
T-bills are commonly viewed as "the" risk-free asset;	
Money market funds - the most accessible risk-free asset for most investors.
Risky asset: stock (or a portfolio) or mutual fund or a particular index fund
Can represent the total investments in risky assets
Examine risk/return tradeoff
Demonstrate how different degrees of risk aversion will affect allocations between risky and risk free assets
notes:
A money market fund is a kind of mutual fund that invests in highly liquid, near-term instruments. These instruments include cash, cash equivalent securities, and high-credit-rating, debt-based securities with a short-term maturity (such as U.S. Treasuries). Money market funds are intended to offer investors high liquidity with a very low level of risk. Money market funds are also called money market mutual funds.

Assume you chose to invest in risky and risk free assets. Risky is a stock or index or mutual fund. We’re not choosing the risky asset at this moment, just the portfolio. 
What is the proportion you’ll invest in risky and risk free assets so that your utility will be maximized. What proportion will you invest in risk free and risky assets? This is capital allocation. Recall that risky will have higher return. 

Allocation between the two is capital allocation

title: CAL (Capital Allocation Line)
notes:
This line is called the capital allocation line. It is used to help investors understand the return of an investment compared to its risk. The ratio is the average return earned in excess of the risk-free rate per unit of volatilityor total risk.


Recall that risk premium is the expected return on the risky asset minus the return from the risk free asset. So were essentially dividing the risk premium from the standard deviation. This is Sharpe  ratio. When doing portfolio optimization this is what you want to maximize. 
Another interpretation is this is the extra return per unit of risk. 

We will talk later abut why we want to maximize the sharpe ratio

Recall You can borrow money using margins to invest in higher risk assets and go further upper right on line to invest more than  100% (y=1) into risky asset. If we use 50% margin we can invest 200%  instead

title: Optimal Allocation
text: Given an investor's risk aversion, how to determine the optimal allocation?
notes:
Where will you choose to invest? Lets say an investors indifference curve is here. 
We know if they only invest in risk free then Utility will be 0.07 (because u = 0.07-.5*A*0) for  this investment opportunity 
Or you can choose to invest at red dot where you’ve invested 75 in risky and 25 in risk free based on CAL line
Which of these two options would you prefer? Youd prefer the one with 75/25 split because it increases utility
We can do better though, what if we choose to invest ant yellow dot. This proportion will increase utility even more. 
Red x isn’t possible we cant achieve this level of utility
IN SUMMARY we want to invest in rf asset and risky portfolio in the ratio that will achieve the highest utility 

So the question is Amoung the feasible choices what is your best capital allocation? 
C is tangent  point of where you should invest. Has highest utility.
What is the relationship between CAL and utility curve? The CAL is the tangent to the highest utility of where you should invest

Why do we care about sharpe ratio? You have two risky asset portfolio options P2 and P1 which risky portfolio would you prefer in this case? We need to know which would do better.
Look at their CALs. Each one is a tangent to a different indifference curve. The indifference curves are all parallel to each other for a single investor (because same A) so investment opportunity with higher slope of CAL will be the tangent of an indifference curve with a larger value. Therefore in this case youd choose risky portfolio P2

You compare the portfiolios using their sharpe ratios if you want to compare the two portfolios quantitatively, its higher for P2 than P1 ebcasue of the slope of CAP.
When choosing a portfolio choose the one with the highest slope to maximize the sharpe ratio.

Each person has their own version of the utility function

title: Extending Concepts to All risky Securities (INSTAD OF JUST 2)
text: Extending Concepts to All risky Securities (INSTAD OF JUST 2)

The optimal combinations result in lowest level of risk for a given return
The optimal trade-off is described as the efficient frontier
These portfolios are dominant
notes:
Now you have many different single securities. What is best choice of portfolio you can use? You can look at combo of different risky assets  here. If we draw a horizontal line it’s the same expected return but we want the lowest risk. If we draw verticlae line there is same risk but we want highest expected return.
So in the general case we always choose the efficient frontier portfolio (upper half)
Frontier portfolio is any portfolio on bound. 

This is similar to the two asset case. 
Not everyone will choose same portfolio because some will want to invest more heavily in rf (x axis  is 0) and others want to infest more in risky. 

If youre risk adverse you wont choose anything inside because youd rather take something with same level of return with lowest risk aka whatever is on the frontier
image_descriptions: Diagram generalizing from two risky assets to many: shows the efficient frontier (upper boundary of the minimum-variance frontier) plotted against many individual assets (dots) inside it, with the global minimum-variance portfolio marked at the leftmost point of the frontier. Illustrates that with many risky assets, the same CAL-tangency logic applies to the efficient frontier as a whole rather than just two assets.
